title: Information geometry of continuum limits in lattice field theory: The Gross-Neveu model with Wilson fermions
abstract: When the Boltzmann weight is nonnegative, the actions of a lattice field theory define a family of probability distributions that forms a statistical manifold, and its Fisher metric gives the number of measurements needed to distinguish two nearby actions. In the large-$N$ limit of the two-dimensional lattice Gross-Neveu model with Wilson fermions, we study the continuum limit, in which the lattice spacing $a$ is taken to zero with the mass gap $Λ$ fixed, through the Fisher metric of the distribution of the auxiliary field $σ$. The renormalization condition fixes an expectation coordinate, and dimensional transmutation becomes an exponential relation between it and a natural coordinate. The main result is that the $a\to0$ limits differ between the Fisher metric of the long-distance modes, whose momenta are fixed in physical units, and the Fisher metric of the full $P(σ)$. In the former, the lengths of the infinitely many irrelevant directions that change the kinetic term shrink, relative to the mass-term direction, to order $aΛ\log(1/(aΛ))$ or smaller, and when several modes are combined, only the two directions $(Λ,m)$ of the continuum theory remain. In the latter, the kinetic-term directions shrink at the same rate as the mass-term direction, and the difference in the regularization remains in correlations at distances of the order of the lattice spacing. An exception is the deformation that only adds a contact term to the propagator: as $a\to0$ its length goes to zero in both metrics, and it becomes indistinguishable from a change of the coupling $1/g^2$ (a lattice version of Kutasov's result). The curvature of the coupling plane at fixed kinetic term diverges as $(1/2)\log^2(1/(aΛ))$, not as the correlation volume often assumed in thermodynamic geometry, and the critical point is infinitely far in Fisher distance from any point at finite $a$.
summary: This theoretical paper uses information geometry to study the continuum limit of the lattice Gross-Neveu model. It finds that the physical result depends on whether one first fixes the long-distance modes or takes the lattice spacing to zero. This non-commutativity highlights subtle, non-trivial aspects of renormalization in lattice field theory.
main_problem: The paper investigates the continuum limit of lattice field theories by analyzing the information geometry defined by the Fisher metric.
main_result: The continuum limit depends on the order in which the lattice spacing ($a 	o 0$) and the physical modes are taken, showing that these limits do not commute.
method: The analysis uses the Fisher metric applied to the probability distribution of an auxiliary field ($\sigma$) derived from the lattice action, comparing metrics derived from long-distance modes versus the full distribution.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the two-dimensional lattice Gross-Neveu model with Wilson fermions in the large-$N$ limit. The theory is analyzed by mapping the lattice action to a statistical manifold.
key_observables: The Fisher metric, the curvature of the coupling plane, and the behavior of the propagator $G(q)$ under different limits.
important_parameters: Lattice spacing ($a$), mass gap ($\Lambda$), and the large-$N$ limit. The analysis involves comparing the long-distance mode metric to the full $P(\sigma)$ metric.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the large-$N$ limit and the use of the auxiliary field $\sigma$ because the Boltzmann weight is not strictly a probability distribution.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the Fisher metric ellipses for long-distance modes versus the full $P(\sigma)$ as $a$ decreases. Other figures illustrate the coupling plane and metric behavior.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares two approaches to the continuum limit: fixing long-distance modes versus taking $a 	o 0$. It derives curvature formulas and analyzes the non-commutativity of these limits using the Fisher metric.
why_interesting: The rigorous study of how physical observables (like the continuum limit) depend on the order of taking limits is a fundamental concern in quantum field theory, relevant for understanding renormalization group flow in many-body systems.
